title: Robotaxi Cameras Put Passenger Privacy Under Scrutiny
summary:
Driverless taxis rely on cameras to navigate, but some cameras face the passengers instead of the road. Reporting by WIRED examines how those interior recordings are used and why privacy specialists want clearer rules.

Companies say cabin cameras help protect riders and enforce service rules. They can also help workers check cleanliness or locate belongings left behind. Waymo employees have used vehicle intercoms to ask passengers whether they were old enough to travel alone, including some adult passengers.

Waymo says automated technology helps its teams identify possible violations. A company patent describes camera systems performing checks before, during and after rides. However, its spokesperson did not confirm whether that particular patented system is being used. A patent describes an invention; it does not establish that the invention is operating in a product.

Zoox says its interior cameras record the entire ride. Its policies allow personal data to support operations and develop or improve its product. The company also says it might record conversations between passengers and support workers, but does not save those conversation recordings.

Tesla's Robotaxi documents say a green indicator appears on the central touchscreen when the camera is active. Riders can opt into sharing cabin video and audio through the app's privacy settings. The documents also say early access participants automatically opt into data sharing. Tesla did not answer WIRED's questions about whether that program had ended.

Waymo, Zoox and Tesla say human staff view interior cameras only when necessary. Their policies also allow personal data, including recordings, to be provided to law enforcement or regulators. Waymo says government agencies seeking data are directed to follow valid legal processes.

Justin Brookman of Consumer Reports says vehicles without drivers need ways to check passenger behavior, but also need limits on monitoring. Privacy experts say few clear US rules govern this kind of surveillance. Matthew Guariglia of the Electronic Frontier Foundation is concerned about companies collecting information and finding reasons to sell it.

Passengers often agree to lengthy app terms before booking. That leaves an important question: what information does a ride collect, and how much control does the passenger have over its later use?
why_it_matters: Cameras can help companies manage driverless rides while collecting passenger information. The article explains why experts want clearer limits on how that information is collected and used.
